entries.meaning: Kali-age renunciants spend heavily adorning their houses because sensuality has stolen detachment; ascetics are wealthy and householders poor. Men expel faithful wives of good family and bring servant-women home. Sons respect parents only until they see a woman's face; once the wife's family becomes dear, their own kin appear as enemies. Sinful kings lack dharma and continually punish and torment their subjects. Wealth alone makes one noble despite impurity; a displayed sacred thread marks a Brahmin and nakedness an ascetic. One who rejects Veda and Purana is called a true saint and servant of Hari. Crowds of poets abound, generosity is unheard of, fault-finders form multitudes and the virtuous do not protest. Famines recur and people die in misery for want of food.

Women have little ornament beyond their hair, and hunger is widespread. The poor are miserable and entangled in many attachments; fools seek happiness without loving dharma, and minds are shallow, harsh and without tenderness. People are afflicted by disease without enjoying life's goods, quarrelling from groundless pride. Life may last scarcely fifteen years, yet pride imagines itself safe until the end of an age. Kali makes people distraught: they do not respect even a younger sister or daughter, and contentment, reflection and calm disappear as every community becomes needy. Envy, harsh speech and greed fill the world; equality is lost, people suffer separation and sorrow, and the conduct of social and spiritual orders collapses. Self-restraint, charity, compassion and understanding are unknown; stupidity and deception multiply. Men and women live merely to sustain the body, and slanderers spread everywhere.

In Satya-yuga, contemplative knowers cross becoming through meditation on Hari; in Treta people cross by offering varied sacrifices and their acts to the Lord; in Dvapara they cross by worshipping Raghupati's feet. In Kali the sole way is to sing Hari's virtues. Yoga, sacrifice and esoteric knowledge are not the support of this age: its one foundation is praise of Rama. Whoever abandons every other reliance, worships Rama and lovingly sings his host of virtues crosses the ocean of becoming without doubt, for the name's power is manifest in Kali. The age has one holy distinction: intentions of merit bear fruit, while merely mental sins do not accrue in the same way.

Prompted by Rama's Maya, the dispositions of all four ages arise continually in every heart. Pure sattva, equanimity and realization, with a serene mind, mark Satya's influence. Much sattva, some rajas and delight in action produce Treta's dharma and happiness. Much rajas, little sattva and some tamas make Dvapara's mixture of joy and fear. Much tamas and a little rajas produce Kali's conflict on every side. The wise discern these inner age-qualities, abandon adharma and love dharma. The age cannot dominate one whose love for Raghupati's feet is intense, just as a magician's illusion cannot overpower the magician's servant.

Bhushundi went to Ujjain poor, soiled, destitute and distressed. In time he acquired some wealth and resumed serving Shiva. A Vedic Brahmin there worshipped Shiva continually, was deeply saintly, understood the highest good and never disparaged Hari. Bhushundi served him deceitfully, but the compassionate and principled Brahmin saw only his outward humility and taught him like a son. The noble Brahmin gave him Shiva's mantra and much good instruction. Bhushundi repeated the mantra in Shiva's temple while pride and self-importance swelled within his heart.

One day the guru summoned Bhushundi and taught him right conduct in many ways: the true fruit of serving Shiva is uninterrupted devotion to Rama's feet, for Shiva and Brahma themselves worship Rama. Hearing the guru call Shiva a servant of Hari burned Bhushundi's heart. Learning in his base condition affected him like milk fed to a snake: proud, crooked and unfortunate, he opposed his guru day and night, while the merciful teacher never grew angry and repeatedly instructed him. Bhushundi illustrates the base person's ingratitude: one first destroys the very benefactor through whom one rose. Smoke born of fire can extinguish fire after becoming a cloud; dust lies despised and trodden on the road, but when wind raises it, it first fills the eyes and crowns of kings. Therefore the wise avoid the wicked, keeping neither quarrel nor friendship with them, as they would avoid a dog. Yet Bhushundi's deceitful heart found no pleasure in his guru's well-meant words.

A voice from the sky resounds through the temple: although Bhushundi's compassionate, clear-sighted guru feels no anger, the Lord will curse this ignorant, arrogant wretch because violation of right order cannot be tolerated; leaving him unpunished would corrupt the scriptural path. Those who envy a guru fall in Raurava hell for millions of ages and then endure pain through ten thousand births among the three worlds' forms. Because Bhushundi sits rigid like a python, the voice commands him to become a serpent and enter the hollow of a great tree, receiving the lowest course.

The guru sings the Rudrashtakam to appease Shiva: he bows to the Lord of liberation, all-pervading Brahman and embodiment of the Veda—self-existent, qualityless, unwavering, desireless, consciousness-space clothed in space; formless source of Om, the transcendent Lord beyond speech, knowledge and senses; terrible Time of time yet compassionate treasury of virtue who carries beings beyond the world. He praises Shiva's snow-mountain radiance, profound beauty beyond countless loves, streaming Ganga, crescent moon and serpent necklace; his moving earrings, noble brows, great eyes, gracious face, blue throat, deerskin and skull-garland; his fierceness, excellence, unborn wholeness and brilliance, the trident-bearing Lord of Bhavani who uproots threefold pain and is reached through devotion. He begs the destroyer of delusion and desire to be gracious, since no peace or release from suffering comes until people worship Uma's Lord; knowing neither yoga, repetition nor worship, he bows always and asks Shiva to protect him from the burning mass of age, birth and pain. The closing verse says Shiva favours those who recite this hymn devotedly. Hearing the plea and seeing the Brahmin's love, the heavenly voice invites a boon. The guru asks first for devotion to Shiva's feet and then begs the compassionate Lord not to be angry with the deluded creature bound by Maya, but to turn the curse into grace within a short time.

words: I bow to Ishana, Lord of lords
a young moon shines upon the brow
destroyer at the end of an age
ever giving joy to the good

entries.meaning: The guru asks the treasury of compassion to do whatever brings Bhushundi's highest welfare. Shiva accepts the selfless plea. Though Bhushundi committed a grave offence and Shiva cursed in anger, the guru's goodness moves him to special grace: forgiving benefactors are as dear to Shiva as Rama. The curse cannot be fruitless, so Bhushundi will undergo a thousand births, but the agony of birth and death will not touch him and his knowledge will never disappear. Because he was born in Raghupati's city and later set his mind on Shiva's service, Ayodhya's influence and Shiva's grace will awaken devotion to Rama in his heart. Service to Brahmins is a vow that pleases Hari; hence he must never insult a Brahmin and should regard saints as forms of the Infinite. One may survive Indra's thunderbolt, Shiva's trident, Time's rod or Vishnu's fierce discus, but the fire of hostility to a Brahmin burns its victim. Keeping this discernment, nothing in the world will be inaccessible to him, and Shiva also grants unobstructed movement.

Whatever body Bhushundi assumes among gods, humans or other beings in the three worlds, he continues worshipping Rama. One pain never leaves him: memory of his guru's gentle character. At last he receives the human Brahmin body praised by Veda and Purana as rare even for gods. As a child he gathers other children and enacts all Raghunayaka's sports. When grown, his father tries repeatedly to teach him, but study, listening and reflection do not please him; every other desire has fled and his mind clings only to Rama's feet. He asks who would abandon the wish-fulfilling cow to serve a common donkey. Immersed in love, he finds nothing else attractive and his father gives up teaching him. When his parents die, he goes to the forest to worship the protector of devotees. Wherever he finds sages, he bows in their hermitages and asks for the depth of Rama's virtues, joyfully wandering as he hears Hari's stories. By Shiva's grace his movement is unhindered; the three powerful cravings fall away and one longing grows—to see Rama's lotus feet and count his birth fulfilled. Each sage teaches that Ishvara pervades every being, but the formless doctrine does not please him, for his heart's love for embodied Brahman is intense.
